## Overview

The Kombe are an African ethnic group and members of the Bantu group. They are indigenous to Equatorial Guinea and are native speakers of the Kombe language, also called Ngumbi. The Kombe are one of the Ndowe peoples of the coast and are associated with the Rio Muni coast. From 1964 to 1969, they were located in Punta Mbonda, north of Bata. They later settled in Cameroon, south of Bata, and south of Rio Benito. They are sometimes referred to as Ndowe or “Playeros,” a Spanish term meaning “beach people.” At the beginning of the twentieth century, some Kombe women intermarried with the Benga people on the Isle of Corisco.

## Music & performance

The sources identify the Kombe as one of the Ndowe peoples of the coast, but provide no further information about music or performance.

## Festivals & rituals

The only historical social practice described is that, at the beginning of the twentieth century, some Kombe women intermarried with the Benga people on the Isle of Corisco.

## Language & religion

The Kombe language, or Ngumbi, is a Coastal Bantu language spoken by the Kombe people of Equatorial Guinea. The Kombe are one of the Ndowe peoples of the coast, and Kombe is mutually intelligible with Yasa.
